items.title: Ali Khan Mahmudabad on ‘Ganga-Jamuni fantasy’, dying languages and democracy online
items.summary: In this Newslaundry interview, Professor Ali Khan Mahmudabad, head of Political Science at Ashoka University and author of Poetry of Belonging , examines how culture, poetry and shared histories have shaped Indian Muslims’ relationship with the country, and what threatens that sense of belonging today. From calling the popular idea of Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb a “postcolonial secular elite fantasy” to warning about the erosion of Hindi and Urdu, Professor Khan challenges familiar narratives about religion, secularism and social harmony. He argues that people did not have to abandon their faiths to live together; they built bonds while remaining deeply rooted in their own religious traditions. He also discusses the rewriting of history, shrinking space for dissent in universities, and how social media is reshaping identity and political discourse. As trolling becomes routine and politics increasingly plays out online, what is at stake for India’s democracy? The conversation also turns to the political scientist’s lineage, the historic estate of Mahmudabad and its rare manuscripts. items.title: South Central 97: Why were journalists being detained and beaten by Delhi Police?
items.summary: Were the police only trying to stop the protests, or also to stop journalists from creating a public record of what happened on the streets? What happens when journalists covering protests are detained by the police, and what does it mean for press freedom and the right to dissent in India? In this week’s South Central, hosts Dhanya Rajendran and Anisha Sheth examine the crackdown’s implications for independent media, press freedom and the right to protest. They are joined by Siddharth Varadarajan, founding editor of The Wire , and Abhinandan Sekhri of Newslaundry , to discuss allegations of police violence, the targeting of journalists documenting the protests, and the lack of a stronger collective response from mainstream media. The discussion examines whether the police were not only trying to prevent protests but also attempting to stop journalists from creating a public record of what happened on the streets. Siddharth Varadarajan argues that journalists documenting police action during earlier protests had brought evidence of violence and excessive force to public attention, and that reporters were targeted this time to prevent similar footage from reaching audiences. items.title: Delhi SEM court grants bail to CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke
items.summary: A Delhi court on Saturday granted bail to Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke. The order was passed by a court of the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM). Dipke's legal team confirmed the development. The Court has imposed certain conditions on him. Details are awaited. Dipke and All India Students’ Association (AISA) president Neha Bora were detained by the Delhi Police on October 16 ahead of the ‘Lehra Do Tiranga’ protest at Connaught Place. Dipke was picked up near his residence while heading to the protest at Connaught Place while Bora was detained while she was marching from Mandi House. Notably, CJP activists Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka are already in judicial custody after they tried to enter Jantar Mantar area. items.title: Rishikanth, female fandom and the fine line between desire and objectification
items.summary: It has been nearly two months since Modha Rathri and 25 days since Dorothy were released. For actor Rishikanth, who starred in both, life hasn't been the same. It has swung from online and offline adoration to what can well be termed harassment in the public space. Rishi’s screen presence as Marudhu and Karthi in the two films has brought in comparisons with Rajinikanth. There’s joy that a Tamil-looking hero is making it big on screen, and he’s receiving overwhelming love from female audiences. However, his boundaries have been quashed, and he’s being seen as a commodity – squished, scratched, hugged forcibly, so much so that on occasions, the team handling him had to pull him up from the thronging crowd and peel female fans off him. items.title: Social media users must be given copy of takedown order: Punjab and Haryana High Court
items.summary: The Punjab and Haryana High Court recently said that authorities ordering takedown of a social media page must also inform the user while notifying the intermediary [Haryana 24 News Network Private Limited v Union of India and Others] Justice Tribhuvan Dahiya made the observation while setting aside an order passed by the Haryana Police directing takedown of the Facebook page of Haryana 24 News Network Private Limited. The Court noted that Rule 3(2) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 does not explicitly lay down the requirement to notify the user whose content or page is ordered to be taken down by the authorities. However, it observed that this requirement is an essential obligation ingrained in the principles of natural justice and has to be read into the rule. “Accordingly, a copy of the intimation must be furnished to the user when it is sent to the intermediary. This will make the procedure of sub-rule (2) to Rule 3 compliant of the primary tenets of natural justice and constitutionally valid,” the Court said.
